description.value: An fMRI study of healthy food decision-making, examining food-versus-activity activation and task-related DMFC/dACC connectivity in relation to food cravings and eating-related self-control.

value: we predicted that greater DMFC/dACC activation would be associated with greater self-reported desire/craving for high-fat foods.

we predicted that, when compared to a non-food-related decision-making task, food-related decision-making would activate the DMFC/dACC and insula, as well as ventral visual regions associated with food perception.
we hypothesized that eating-related self-control would be diminished as connectivity between the insula and DMFC/dACC became more negative

value: The Food > Activities contrast revealed significant activations within a large cluster encompassing the DMFC/dACC region bilaterally, as well as clusters within the right anterior insula, left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, two left hemisphere regions of the ventral visual cortex, the left anterior insula, the left motor/premotor cortex, and the right posterior insula.
Greater DMFC/dACC activation was associated with greater self-reported cravings for high-fat foods and greater desire to eat the high-fat/high-calorie foods depicted in the unhealthy food images.

The observed DMFC/dACC activation was interpreted as reflecting greater response conflict when choosing healthy food options in individuals who found competing unhealthy food options more salient or rewarding.

spans.text: For the contrast of Food > Activities, our seed-to-voxel gPPI analysis using the DMFC/dACC cluster (i.e., from the standard fMRI analysis reported in Table 1 ) as a seed region revealed significantly negative connectivity between the DMFC/dACC cluster and both the right AI and the right precuneus (see Table 2 and Fig. 1b ).

model_representation_notes.value: gPPI analyses do not justify conclusions about the direction of influence between regions; the negative connectivity reflects a relationship over and above task-related activation differences but does not establish that the insula inhibits the DMFC/dACC or vice versa.

spans.text: It is important to highlight that gPPI analyses do not justify conclusions about the direction of influence between two regions (McLaren et al. 2012 ); gPPI methodology accounts for task-related changes when assessing the relationship between activity in two regions (thus only detecting a relationship over and above those attributable to task-related changes in activation), but it does not provide causal information.
